title: Tensorflow dll load failing
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow Windows DLL import-order failure has a concrete workaround, anchored by duplicate issue #91656 and the sitecustomize.py workaround the reporter provided.
security_topic: Windows DLL/runtime initialization conflict causing import-order failure
question_text:
The order of imports causes issues in tensorflow. If tensorflow isn't imported first, it results with dll load error.

If I import pandas first it gives the dll error. 

When running in jupyter lab, if I import tensorflow in the first cell, it also fails with the same error.

This was working in tensorflow 2.14.0. In the recent migration we faced this issue. The same error is also seen in 2.19.0 and 2.18.0 as well.
answer_text:
This issue appears related to the Windows DLL/runtime initialization conflict already being tracked in #91656, including similar import-order and dependency loading failures observed on Windows environments.
To keep the discussion consolidated and avoid duplicate tracking, I am closing this issue as a duplicate of #91656.

title: bug in TensorFlow when using API `tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset`
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow crash in `tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset` is resolved by the proposed fixes in PR #107295 and PR #107384.
security_topic: runtime crash from async kernel handling in table initialization
question_text: I encountered a bug in TensorFlow when I used API `tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset`.
answer_text:
I was able to reproduce the same crash with TensorFlow [2.19.0 and 2.20.0](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/8680f6451be83e3ff3e9f874018923c0/107125_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v.ipynb) on CPU, where `tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset` causes the runtime to abort instead of raising a Python exception. As you pointed out, this appears to be related to an async kernel implementation (AsAsync() check failure), which should be handled more gracefully.
A fix for this issue has already been proposed in the form of [few](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/pull/107295) [PRs](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/pull/107384). Once the fix is merged, this crash should be resolved in upcoming TensorFlow releases.

I encountered a bug in TensorFlow when I used API `tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset`. The code is as follows:

```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Create a dummy dataset
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: (x, x * 2))

# Create a table
keys = tf.constant([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype=tf.int64)
values = tf.constant([0, 0, 0, 0, 0], dtype=tf.int64)
table = tf.lookup.StaticHashTable(
    tf.lookup.KeyValueTensorInitializer(keys, values), default_value=-1
)

# Initialize table from dataset
tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset(
    table_handle=table.resource_handle,
    dataset=dataset._variant_tensor
)
```

The error message was as follows:

```shell
Check failed: nullptr == ctx->params_->op_kernel->AsAsync()
Use OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC in AsyncOpKernel implementations.
Aborted (core dumped)
```

The above code causes the TensorFlow runtime to abort instead of raising a Python exception. The issue is reproducible on CPU using TensorFlow 2.19. Here is the [gist](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1qf92A78AOPH_XqoG5Z9JssB7DXCQsPEw?usp=sharing).

# Create a dummy dataset

# Create a table
keys = tf.constant([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype=tf.int64)
values = tf.constant([0, 0, 0, 0, 0], dtype=tf.int64)
table = tf.lookup.StaticHashTable(
    tf.lookup.KeyValueTensorInitializer(keys, values), default_value=-1
)

# Initialize table from dataset
tf.raw_ops.InitializeTableFromDataset(
    table_handle=table.resource_handle,
    dataset=dataset._variant_tensor
)
```

Use OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC in AsyncOpKernel implementations.

title: [CUDA] illegal memory read on Svd
need_summary: Whether the CUDA Svd out-of-bounds read on a 46341×46341 input is caused by exceeding GPU memory and kernel indexing limits, as explained in TensorFlow maintainer comment c1.
security_topic: GPU SVD out-of-bounds read on oversized tensor input
question_text:
### Current behavior?

Compute-Sanitizer reports an out of bounds read on SwapDimension1And2InTensor3UsingTiles
answer_text:
Hi @kokol16 ,
Apologies for the delay, and thanks for the report. The issue occurs because the input to` tf.raw_ops.Svd` is extremely large:
```
[46341, 46341]
```
This matrix contains over 2.1 billion float32 elements, requiring about 8.6 GB just for the input tensor. GPU-based SVD needs several additional temporary buffers, so the total memory requirement can exceed 30–50 GB.

Such matrix sizes exceed both GPU memory capacity and the internal indexing limits of the tiling kernel (SwapDimension1And2InTensor3UsingTiles). As a result, the kernel computes invalid tile offsets and performs out-of-bounds memory reads, which is why Compute-Sanitizer reports an error. When a reasonable matrix size is used (e.g., 512×512, 1024×1024, etc.), the SVD op works correctly. TensorFlow should ideally raise a clear ResourceExhaustedError instead of allowing the kernel to proceed with invalid dimensions, so your report highlights a missing validation check.
I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/b482899057b5951944586cf3a04f71bd/104359_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) with a smaller, valid example for your reference. Hope this clarifies the issue.

title: [CUDA] illegal memory read on SparseConcat
need_summary: Whether invalid SparseTensor inputs can trigger the reported out-of-bounds GPU read in SparseConcat, and the answer rests on the maintainer’s explanation in comment c1 plus the attached valid-example gist.
security_topic: validity of SparseTensor inputs causing GPU memory read warning
question_text: Compute-Sanitizer reports an out of bounds read on DeviceRadixSortSingleTileKernel
answer_text:
The problem is caused by invalid SparseTensor inputs, rather than an issue with the SparseConcat op itself. In your code, I noticed the following:
- The indices contain extremely large negative values (-9223372036854775808), but SparseTensor indices must always be non-negative and within the bounds of the corresponding dense shape.
- You specified shapes [0, 0, 0] for both tensors, which means the dense tensors have zero volume. A SparseTensor with shape (0, 0, 0) cannot contain any entries, yet each of your tensors has 3 values. This makes the indices, values, and shapes inconsistent. Because these inputs violate SparseTensor invariants, the internal CUB sort kernel receives invalid data and attempts to read from invalid memory, which triggers the out-of-bounds read reported by Compute-Sanitizer.

When valid indices, values, and shapes are used, SparseConcat works correctly. I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/a5628c3dad24ce0c6192076eb05c5369/104260_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) with a valid example for your reference. I hope this clarifies the issue.

title: [CUDA] illegal memory access on segment_sum
need_summary: Whether the CUDA segment_sum invalid-memory-access issue is caused by out-of-range, negative segment_ids and the answer rests on the maintainer’s explanation plus the linked Colab gist.
security_topic: GPU out-of-bounds write from invalid segment IDs
question_text: Compute-Sanitizer reports an invalid atomic operation on SortedSegmentReductionCustomKernel
answer_text:
The problem is caused by invalid values passed to `segment_ids`. For `tf.math.segment_sum`, the `segment_ids` tensor must:
```
be sorted in ascending order,
contain only non-negative integers,
and have values in the range [0, num_segments - 1].
```
In your code, `segment_ids` contains very large negative values (e.g., -21168624) and very large positive values (e.g., 32582). These indices do not correspond to any valid segment for your input, which has only 6 rows. Because of these invalid values, the GPU kernel attempts to perform atomic updates on memory locations outside the valid output buffer, which leads to the out-of-bounds atomic write reported by `Compute-Sanitizer`.

When valid segment IDs are used, the op works correctly. I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/02e7deed531bff812a0a505c9d94cc7b/104258_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) for your reference. I hope this clarifies your issue.

var = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([10, 0], dtype=tf.float32))

Hi @kokol16 ,
Apologies for the delay, and thanks for raising your concern here.
The error occurs due to invalid inputs passed to the `ResourceScatterUpdate` op. In your code, you have:
```
var = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([10, 0], dtype=tf.float32))
indices = tf.constant(-9223372036854775808, dtype=tf.int64)
```
For a variable with shape [10, …], the valid index range is from 0 to 9.

Additionally, var has shape [10, 0], which means each slice contains zero elements.
However, your updates tensor has shape (5,), which is incompatible with the variable’s slice shape. Because of these invalid inputs, the GPU kernel receives incorrect pointers and attempts to write to address `0x0`, which leads to the out-of-bounds write detected by Compute-Sanitizer.

When valid shapes and valid index values are used, the op works correctly. I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/c98d1e909b164f77556a4ebeab67db25/104080_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) for your reference.

title: [CUDA] illegal memory read on  ResourceScatterNdUpdate
need_summary: Whether the CUDA out-of-bounds read in ResourceScatterNdUpdate is caused by empty indices/updates tensors and that the documented shape requirements (`indices` shape `[N, index_depth]`, `updates` shape `[N] + var_shape[index_depth:]`, with `N > 0`) explain the issue.
security_topic: GPU out-of-bounds read in scatter update with empty tensors
question_text: Compute-Sanitizer reports an out of bounds read on ScatterNdOpKernel
answer_text:
The main cause of the problem is the shapes you passed to `indices` and `updates`. Both tensors were created with shape `[0]`, which means they are empty. `ResourceScatterNdUpdate` requires:
```
indices to have shape [N, index_depth]
updates to have shape [N] + var_shape[index_depth:]
and N > 0
```
Since the tensors are empty, the GPU kernel receives invalid pointers and ends up reading from address `0x0`, which causes the out-of-bounds read reported by Compute-Sanitizer.

When I replaced the empty tensors with valid shapes, the op worked correctly. I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/84d905b9cbb5bde9726ac7c4ff317f26/104079_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) for your reference. I hope this helps clarify the issue.

title: [CUDA] illegal memory read on ResourceApplyAdadelta
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow GPU out-of-bounds read in ResourceApplyAdadelta is caused by the zero-sized `accum_update` input, as explained in the maintainer’s shape-mismatch diagnosis and validated by the referenced Colab gist.
security_topic: GPU kernel out-of-bounds read due to shape mismatch in optimizer op
question_text:
### Current behavior?

Compute-Sanitizer reports an out of bounds read on EigenMetaKernel
answer_text:
Hi @kokol16 ,
Apologies for the delay, and thank you for raising this issue.
The main cause of the problem is that `accum_update` is created with a zero-sized shape:
```
accum_update = tf.Variable(tf.zeros([0, 1, 9, 0], dtype=tf.float16))
```
`ResourceApplyAdadelta` requires `var`, `accum`, and `accum_update` to have the same shape. In your example, `var` and `accum` are scalars, while `accum_update` is an empty tensor. Because of this shape mismatch, the GPU kernel attempts to access memory that does not exist, which leads to the out-of-bounds read reported by Compute-Sanitizer.

I tested the same code using a valid scalar values for accum_update, and the op works correctly. I am attaching a colab [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/f006dec48643ae14d9b1469d0b9b6d80/104078_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) for your reference. Hope this clarifies the issue.
Thank you!

The root cause is the extremely large shape value (2147483647). This exceeds the supported int32 dimension limits and also requires more memory than the GPU can allocate. Because of that, the operation goes out of bounds. When I tested with smaller shape values (for example: 21474), the op worked correctly without any errors.

I am attaching a [Colab gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/Venkat6871/238fe2f4ea92635d145645db58ed140c/104076_tf_2-19-0-2-20-0-v-gpu.ipynb) for your reference where you can check the behavior with smaller shapes.

title: Tensorflow lite reference kernel ReduceSum overflows when network type not uint8
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow Lite reference ReduceSum integer overflow bug is still present in LiteRT, with the answer anchored by the linked LiteRT issue #4079.
security_topic: quantized ReduceSum overflow in TFLite/LiteRT reference kernel
question_text:
**System information**
- Linux Ubuntu 22.04
- TensorFlow installed from pip source
- TensorFlow version 2.19.1 
- TFLite runtime installed from pip source
- TFLite runtime version 2.14.0


**Standalone code to reproduce the issue** 

```
import numpy as np
from tflite_runtime.interpreter import Interpreter
from tflite_runtime.interpreter import OpResolverType

interpreter = Interpreter(model_path="minimal.tflite", experimental_op_resolver_type=OpResolverType.BUILTIN_REF)
interpreter.allocate_tensors()

inp = interpreter.get_input_details()[0]
out = interpreter.get_output_details()[0]

x = np.full(inp["shape"], 2, dtype=inp["dtype"])
interpreter.set_tensor(inp["index"], x)
interpreter.invoke()
y = interpreter.get_tensor(out["index"])
print(y)
```

The example network can be created from the attached file minimal.json. The network contains a single ReduceSum Op, the input tensor has shape and type int8[1,128].

Output is [[-1]] when it should be [[127]]

title: [Bug] CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX on new RTX 5080 GPU with Driver 581.29
need_summary: Whether TensorFlow’s RTX 5080 Blackwell PTX failure is a known issue and what workaround helps, based on the linked tracking issue https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/89272 and the documented advice to disable XLA/JIT compilation.
security_topic: GPU PTX/JIT compatibility on Blackwell RTX 5080
question_text:
Current Behavior
When attempting to run any TensorFlow operation on the GPU that requires JIT compilation (e.g., tf.matmul), the execution fails with an InternalError.
The detailed log output reveals that the root cause is a CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX error, which occurs during the cuModuleLoadData step. This initial failure prevents the creation of a valid CUDA function handle, leading to the subsequent and final CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE error when TensorFlow tries to launch the kernel.
This behavior is consistently reproducible on a new NVIDIA RTX 5080 Laptop GPU with the latest drivers, and occurs with both TensorFlow versions 2.20.0 and 2.16.2 installed from pip.
answer_text:
The root cause appears to be that the current TensorFlow pip binaries do not include precompiled CUDA kernels for the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture (Compute Capability 12.0, used in the RTX 50 series).
As a result, when TensorFlow falls back to JIT compilation from PTX, the generated PTX code is rejected by the CUDA 13.x driver, leading to `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX` and `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE` errors.

This is a known and ongoing issue. Please refer to the following tracking [issue](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/89272) for further updates and technical discussions. Some of the comments there may also be helpful for your setup.

The issue seems indeed related to the lack of precompiled kernels for Compute Capability 12.0 (Blackwell) and XLA compilation failures with the new drivers. However, I managed to get a stable training loop and inference running by explicitly disabling XLA devices and JIT compilation. **Workaround that worked for me:** 1. **Disable XLA Devices** (Must be done before importing TensorFlow): ```python import os os.environ['TF_XLA_FLAGS'] = '--tf_xla_enable_xla_devices=false' os.environ['TF_JIT_PROFILING'] = 'false' import tensorflow as tf ``` 2. **Disable JIT in Keras models:** When compiling your model, explicitly set `jit_compile=False`: ```python model.compile( optimizer='adam', loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'], jit_compile=False # Crucial for RTX 5080 stability currently ) ``` With these settings, I am able to utilize the GPU for training without the `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX` crash. --- [c6] @MichaeLaudrup 2026-03-06T17:33:25Z: Hi, I think that this could help: https://github.com/MichaeLaudrup/Artificial_Intelligence_Msc/blob/main/TFM_education_ai_analytics/docs/BLACKWELL_GPU.md ---

The detailed log output reveals that the root cause is a CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX error, which occurs during the cuModuleLoadData step. This initial failure prevents the creation of a valid CUDA function handle, leading to the subsequent and final CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE error when TensorFlow tries to launch the kernel.
This behavior is consistently reproducible on a new NVIDIA RTX 5080 Laptop GPU with the latest drivers, and occurs with both TensorFlow versions 2.20.0 and 2.16.2 installed from pip.
Key log line:
Expected Behavior
The expected behavior is that the tf.matmul operation should execute successfully on the GPU.
Specifically:
TensorFlow should correctly generate a valid PTX kernel for the new GPU architecture.
The NVIDIA driver should accept this PTX code and successfully JIT-compile it into native SASS.
The operation should complete without any InternalError, CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX, or CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE exceptions.
After the initial (and expected) JIT compilation delay, subsequent calls to the same operation should be fast.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf
import os
import sys
import traceback

# Suppress oneDNN INFO messages to keep the log clean
os.environ['TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS'] = '0'

def run_gpu_check():
    """
    Checks TensorFlow GPU availability and performs a simple computation.
    """
    print("--- System Info ---")
    print("TensorFlow Version:", tf.__version__)
    print("Python Version:", ".".join(map(str, sys.version_info[:3])))
    
    physical_gpus = tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')
    print("Physical GPUs Found:", physical_gpus)
    
    if not physical_gpus:
        print("\nERROR: No GPU detected by TensorFlow.")
        return
    
    print("-------------------")

    try:
        print("\nAttempting a simple GPU computation (tf.matmul)...")
        # Use a smaller tensor to ensure the test runs quickly once fixed
        with tf.device('/GPU:0'):
            a = tf.random.normal((100, 100))
            b = tf.random.normal((100, 100))
            c = tf.matmul(a, b)
            # Ensure the computation is actually executed
            _ = c.numpy()
        
        print("\n✅ GPU computation check PASSED.")
        print("Result tensor was successfully computed on device:", c.device)

    except Exception as e:
        print("\n❌ GPU computation check FAILED.")
        print("   Error Type:", type(e).__name__)
        print("\n   Full Error Traceback:")
        traceback.print_exc()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_gpu_check()
```

comments.author: Venkat6871
comments.body:
Hi @tgshen ,
Thank you for raising this issue.
The root cause appears to be that the current TensorFlow pip binaries do not include precompiled CUDA kernels for the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture (Compute Capability 12.0, used in the RTX 50 series).
As a result, when TensorFlow falls back to JIT compilation from PTX, the generated PTX code is rejected by the CUDA 13.x driver, leading to `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX` and `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE` errors.

This is a known and ongoing issue. Please refer to the following tracking [issue](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/89272) for further updates and technical discussions. Some of the comments there may also be helpful for your setup.

Thank you!

comments.author: YoranWandelsStudentHowest
comments.body:
I can confirm encountering this exact issue on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 GPU using TensorFlow 2.16+. The issue seems indeed related to the lack of precompiled kernels for Compute Capability 12.0 (Blackwell) and XLA compilation failures with the new drivers.

However, I managed to get a stable training loop and inference running by explicitly disabling XLA devices and JIT compilation.

**Workaround that worked for me:**

1. **Disable XLA Devices** (Must be done before importing TensorFlow):
   ```python
   import os
   os.environ['TF_XLA_FLAGS'] = '--tf_xla_enable_xla_devices=false'
   os.environ['TF_JIT_PROFILING'] = 'false'
   
   import tensorflow as tf

```

2. **Disable JIT in Keras models:**
When compiling your model, explicitly set `jit_compile=False`:
```python
model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy'],
    jit_compile=False  # Crucial for RTX 5080 stability currently
)

```



With these settings, I am able to utilize the GPU for training without the `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_PTX` crash.

security_topic: applicability of a CVE fix to remaining integer-width fields
question_text:
To address [CVE-2022-23559](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-23559), commit [1de4972](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/commit/1de49725a5fc4e48f1a3b902ec3599ee99283043) changed `embedding_size` and `lookup_size` from `int` to `size_t`.

I was surprised, however, that the variables `current_output_offset` (line 210 after the commit), `output_offset` (line 233), and `example_embedding_offset` (line 251) were left as `int`, when all can store a product of the now `size_t` `embedding_size` and some other `int`. Unless I am mistaken, these variables (and maybe some I missed) also need to be updated to `size_t`.

title: Issue while converting a model with GRU to .tflite
need_summary: Whether TensorFlow Lite Micro supports a GRU converted with unroll=False, and the answer points to the official supported-operators list and LiteRT Microcontrollers documentation.
security_topic: runtime support limitations for GRU/while-loop models in TFLM
question_text: One question I have here is, when unroll is set to false, the network will have while() operator. Why TFLM is not able to run this model? When I debugged it, I saw the concatenate() operator is getting different dimension (not at axis). Does TFLM supports GRU?
answer_text:
TensorFlow Lite Micro (TFLM) does NOT support GRU operators when `unroll=False` because this configuration generates `while()` operators that are incompatible with TFLM's architecture. The concatenation dimension mismatch you're experiencing is a direct consequence of TFLM's inability to handle dynamic tensor shapes within while loop contexts. Please refer complete and current [list of supported operators](https://github.com/tensorflow/tflite-micro/blob/main/tensorflow/lite/micro/micro_mutable_op_resolver.h) and limitations of LiteRT for Microcontrollers (Previously known as TFLM) [official documentation ](https://ai.google.dev/edge/litert/microcontrollers/overview)

I would recommend you GRU layer to force unrolling by setting `unroll=True` or else go with supported LSTM Operators if that is feasible for your use case or project

[c2] @gaikwadrahul8 2025-08-06T14:43:42Z:
Hi, @ckmadhira 
Thank you for bringing this issue to our attention, As far I know The unroll and stateful arguments in a Keras GRU layer have distinct effects on the generated TFLite model particularly impacting its control flow and quantization behavior.

The unroll argument modifies how a sequence is processed within a single inference call. By default (unroll=False) Keras uses a `tf.while_loop` which appears as a WHILE op in TFLite. This is efficient for handling sequences of varying lengths. When you set unroll=True Keras eliminates this loop and instead replicates the GRU's fundamental operations (matrix multiplications, additions) for each time step in the sequence. This creates a larger, static graph without a WHILE op which can be faster for short, fixed-length sequences but increases model size. The stateful argument controls how the GRU's hidden state is managed between separate inference calls. This is the critical factor impacting quantization.

With stateful=True option the model must preserve its internal hidden state (a float tensor) from one call to the next. During INT8 quantization the TFLite converter must handle this float state within an otherwise integer-based graph. To do so, it inserts Quantize and Dequantize operations around the state related calculations. This is why you observe a mixed-precision model with some float32 operations remaining they are necessary to maintain the state's precision and continuity across inferences.

On the other hand with `stateful=False` the GRU's state is reset for each new input. Since there is no persistent state to manage between calls the quantization process is greatly simplified. The TFLite converter can transform the entire model into a pure INT8 graph as there's no need to dequantize to float32 for state management. This results in a fully quantized often more performant model.

If full integer quantization proves challenging please consider alternative post-training quantization methods like `float16` quantization for reduced model size with minimal accuracy loss or `dynamic range quantization` which quantizes weights to int8 while activations are dynamically quantized at inference time often suitable for RNNs.

If I have missed something here please let me know. Thank you for your cooperation and understanding.

comments.author: gaikwadrahul8
comments.body:
Hi, @ckmadhira 
Thank you for bringing this issue to our attention, As far I know The unroll and stateful arguments in a Keras GRU layer have distinct effects on the generated TFLite model particularly impacting its control flow and quantization behavior.

The unroll argument modifies how a sequence is processed within a single inference call. By default (unroll=False) Keras uses a `tf.while_loop` which appears as a WHILE op in TFLite. This is efficient for handling sequences of varying lengths. When you set unroll=True Keras eliminates this loop and instead replicates the GRU's fundamental operations (matrix multiplications, additions) for each time step in the sequence. This creates a larger, static graph without a WHILE op which can be faster for short, fixed-length sequences but increases model size. The stateful argument controls how the GRU's hidden state is managed between separate inference calls. This is the critical factor impacting quantization.

With stateful=True option the model must preserve its internal hidden state (a float tensor) from one call to the next. During INT8 quantization the TFLite converter must handle this float state within an otherwise integer-based graph. To do so, it inserts Quantize and Dequantize operations around the state related calculations. This is why you observe a mixed-precision model with some float32 operations remaining they are necessary to maintain the state's precision and continuity across inferences.

On the other hand with `stateful=False` the GRU's state is reset for each new input. Since there is no persistent state to manage between calls the quantization process is greatly simplified. The TFLite converter can transform the entire model into a pure INT8 graph as there's no need to dequantize to float32 for state management. This results in a fully quantized often more performant model.

If full integer quantization proves challenging please consider alternative post-training quantization methods like `float16` quantization for reduced model size with minimal accuracy loss or `dynamic range quantization` which quantizes weights to int8 while activations are dynamically quantized at inference time often suitable for RNNs.

If I have missed something here please let me know. Thank you for your cooperation and understanding.

comments.author: gaikwadrahul8
comments.body:
Hi, @ckmadhira
TensorFlow Lite Micro (TFLM) does NOT support GRU operators when `unroll=False` because this configuration generates `while()` operators that are incompatible with TFLM's architecture. The concatenation dimension mismatch you're experiencing is a direct consequence of TFLM's inability to handle dynamic tensor shapes within while loop contexts. Please refer complete and current [list of supported operators](https://github.com/tensorflow/tflite-micro/blob/main/tensorflow/lite/micro/micro_mutable_op_resolver.h) and limitations of LiteRT for Microcontrollers (Previously known as TFLM) [official documentation ](https://ai.google.dev/edge/litert/microcontrollers/overview)

I would recommend you GRU layer to force unrolling by setting `unroll=True` or else go with supported LSTM Operators if that is feasible for your use case or project 

Thank you for your cooperation and understanding.

title: [RNN] Conversion of model containing GRU layer to quantized TFLite causes Segmentation Fault
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow Lite quantized GRU conversion segfault is a known limitation and what workaround or version guidance applies, anchored by the maintainer’s comment that full integer quantization conflicts with GRU state management and the later recommendation to try newer versions or LiteRT.
security_topic: full integer quantization crash in GRU/TFLite conversion
question_text:
Dear @gaikwadrahul8 

I really need the model to be fully quantized so I am interested if there are plans to fix the broken feature in the converter.

Best Regards
answer_text:
The error occurs because GRU layers have complex state management that conflicts with full integer quantization so if full integer quantization is not compulsary for your use case/ project you can go with either float16 Quantization or dynamic range quantization which is more compatible with RNN layers.

This is a limitation in the TensorFlow Lite quantization system when dealing with complex recurrent structures. GRU and LSTM layers involve internal states and complex cell implementations that the quantization process sometimes cannot properly handle resulting in segmentation faults during model calibration. I have tried from my end with float16 Quantization and dynamic range quantization it's working as expected for your reference here is [gist-file](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/gaikwadrahul8/f3bbece55e498d1291e36ab09f29b46e/tflite-87468-issue.ipynb)

Hi, @knebojsa11
I apologize for the delay in my response, The error occurs because GRU layers have complex state management that conflicts with full integer quantization so if full integer quantization is not compulsary for your use case/ project you can go with either float16 Quantization or dynamic range quantization which is more compatible with RNN layers. 

This is a limitation in the TensorFlow Lite quantization system when dealing with complex recurrent structures. title: Buffer allocation error in Tensorflow Lite with OpenCL backend on certain platforms
need_summary: Whether the OpenCL buffer allocation overflow in TensorFlow Lite on macOS was fixed by PR #87584, which the maintainer said would resolve the >2GB allocation issue.
security_topic: integer truncation causing oversized OpenCL buffer allocation
question_text:
### Current behavior?

I noticed a memory allocation error in clCreateBuffer. The issue seems to be caused by this:

1) TFlite tries to alloca 0xa2000000 bytes of memory (value stored as size_t)

2) The call ends up in this function (tensorflow/lite/experimental/litert/runtime/opencl/buffer.cc):

```
absl::Status CreateClBuffer(cl_context context, int size_in_bytes,
                            bool read_only, void* data, cl_mem* result) 
```

where the size is now int (i.e. 32 bit signed integer... so 0xa2000000 is interpreted as a negative value).

3) This function then calls clCreateBuffer, which takes the size argument as size_t again, and thus receives 0xffffffffa2000000, i.e. the signed 32 bit integer first sign extended to 64bit and then interpreted as unsigned, and thus resulting in a huge size.

The issue doesn't seem to appear with the same model on Android, probably because: The max buffer allocation size on macOS (M1) seems to be 9GB (according to clinfo), but on that android device it's only 1GB (so on android tflite never tries to allocate such a huge chunk of memory).
answer_text: I believe this PR will fix your issue: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/pull/87584. Thanks for your help.

title: Could not get sample weight from customized loss
need_summary: Whether TensorFlow can use a custom weighted R² objective in `model.fit()` and why the maintainer says it should be negated because `model.fit()` minimizes the loss, supported by the Keras custom-loss docs and the explanation in `compute_loss()`.
security_topic: custom loss handling for sample weights
question_text:
In torch, we could easily use customize loss to calcualte weighted_r2_loss. Example code as below
```
class WeightedR2Loss(nn.Module):
    """PyTorch loss function for weighted R²."""
    def __init__(self, epsilon: float = 1e-38) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the WeightedR2Loss class.

        Args:
            epsilon (float, optional): Small constant added to the denominator 
                for numerical stability. Defaults to 1e-38.
        """
        super(WeightedR2Loss, self).__init__()
        self.epsilon = epsilon

    def forward(
        self,
        y_pred: torch.Tensor,
        y_true: torch.Tensor,
        weights: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Compute the weighted R² loss.

        Args:
            y_true (torch.Tensor): Ground truth tensor.
            y_pred (torch.Tensor): Predicted tensor.
            weights (torch.Tensor): Weights for each observation (same shape as y_true).

        Returns:
            torch.Tensor: Computed weighted R² loss.
        """
        numerator = torch.sum(weights * (y_pred - y_true) ** 2)
        denominator = torch.sum(weights * (y_true) ** 2) + 1e-38
        loss = numerator / denominator
        return loss
```
Hope tf could provide similar solution to solve the problem.
answer_text:
@henghamao 
Thank you for going over your use case in detail. You can do this in Tensorflow by subclassing `keras.Model` and overriding the `compute_loss()` function.

```
class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

    def compute_loss(self, x, y_true, y_pred, sample_weight):
        y_true = tf.cast(y_true, tf.float32)
        y_pred = tf.cast(y_pred, tf.float32)
        sample_weight = tf.cast(sample_weight, tf.float32)
        
        weighted_squared_error = sample_weight * (y_true - y_pred) ** 2
        weighted_true_squared = sample_weight * y_true ** 2
        
        numerator = tf.reduce_sum(weighted_squared_error)
        denominator = tf.reduce_sum(weighted_true_squared)
        
        r2_score = 1 - numerator / denominator
        return r2_score
```

def build_model():
    metrics = ['mae']
    output_num = 1
    inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(40, 36))
    lstm_out = tf.keras.layers.LSTM(32, return_sequences=False)(inputs)
    output = Dense(output_num, activation='linear')(lstm_out)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, output)
    class_weights = {0: 0.3, 1: 2.5, 2: 3.2}
    model.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(), metrics=metrics)
    model.summary()
    return model


def data_gen(class_weights):
    while True:
        x_batch = np.random.rand(128, 40, 36)
        y_batch = np.random.randint(0, 3, (128, 1))
        # Apply class weights to the labels
        sample_weights = np.vectorize(lambda x: class_weights[x])(y_batch)
        yield x_batch, y_batch, sample_weights

model = build_model()
cw = {0: 0.3, 1: 2.5, 2: 3.2}
model.fit(data_gen(cw), epochs=2, steps_per_epoch=10)
```

@henghamao 
This is down to the objective chosen for optimization. The model.fit() call tries to **minimize** the loss. r2 on the other hand should increase when the model performs better. A naive way to do this is by providing the negative of r2. 
More importantly, r2 is not differentiable. So ideally, it shouldn't be used as a loss function for gradient descent, but it can be used as a metric. Something like MSE or MAE would be a better loss function.

title: tensorflow-opt-cuda: error running on Linux via GPU
need_summary: Whether the TensorFlow GPU crash on Manjaro was caused by a CUDA/cuDNN compatibility issue and was resolved by switching to tf-nightly[and-cuda] or the stable tensorflow[and-cuda] package.
security_topic: GPU plugin registration crash and version compatibility
question_text: What am I doing wrong?
answer_text:
The message disappeared in tf-nightly 2.20.0.dev20250305. It can be installed by the following command:
`pip install tf-nightly[and-cuda]`

[c1] @micedevai 2024-12-21T02:30:18Z:
The error you're encountering seems to be a combination of issues related to the CUDA environment, TensorFlow, and possibly mismatches in library versions on Manjaro. The crash (Exit Code 134, signal 6: SIGABRT) typically points to a problem in the underlying system, often a segmentation fault, memory corruption, or an internal assert failure.

Here are some steps to troubleshoot and potentially resolve the issue:

### 1. **Verify TensorFlow with GPU Setup**
   - Ensure TensorFlow can detect your GPU correctly. You can run the following snippet to check if TensorFlow sees your GPU:

   ```python
   import tensorflow as tf
   print("Num GPUs Available: ", len(tf.config.experimental.list_physical_devices('GPU')))
   ```

   If the output is `0`, it means TensorFlow is not able to access your GPU, and this could be the reason you're getting the crash.

### 2. **Check cuDNN, cuBLAS, cuFFT Initialization Issues**
   The logs suggest that TensorFlow is struggling to register cuDNN, cuBLAS, and cuFFT plugins. These are crucial for accelerated computation on NVIDIA GPUs.

   - **cuDNN Version Mismatch**: The error message about registering the cuDNN factory usually occurs when there are conflicts in the cuDNN versions installed on the system. Since you have CUDA 12.4 installed, ensure that you also have the compatible cuDNN version installed.
   
   - Try running this command to ensure you have the correct versions of both CUDA and cuDNN:
   
     ```bash
     pacman -S nvidia-cuda-toolkit nvidia-cudnn
     ```

   - **TensorFlow Compatibility**: Verify that the version of TensorFlow you're using is compatible with your installed CUDA and cuDNN versions. According to the TensorFlow release notes, TensorFlow 2.18.0 is compatible with CUDA 11.2 or 11.8. Since you're using CUDA 12.4, this could be causing issues. You might want to either:
     - Downgrade your CUDA/cuDNN version to match TensorFlow's supported versions.
     - Alternatively, try using a nightly build of TensorFlow that might support newer CUDA versions.

### 3. **Memory Issues / GPU Overload**
   The assertion error and core dump could also indicate a memory issue. The RTX 4090 is a powerful GPU, but there could still be memory overloads or memory leaks in the TensorFlow code. 

   Try limiting the GPU memory growth using the following configuration before running your TensorFlow code:

   ```python
   physical_devices = tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')
   tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth(physical_devices[0], True)
   ```

### 4. **Update TensorFlow and Dependencies**
   Ensure you're using the latest stable version of TensorFlow compatible with your system. Since you're on Manjaro, it's possible that some dependencies might be outdated or incompatible.

   Run the following commands to update your system and TensorFlow dependencies:

   ```bash
   sudo pacman -Syu        # Update system
   pip install --upgrade tensorflow
   pip install --upgrade numpy
   pip install --upgrade keras
   ```

   If you're still using the `python-tensorflow-opt-cuda` binary package from `pacman`, consider switching to the `pip`-based TensorFlow installation as the Manjaro package might be outdated or incorrectly configured.

### 5. **Testing with CPU Only**
   If the issue is specifically with GPU support, you can try disabling GPU usage temporarily to verify if the issue is related to CUDA. This can be done by setting the environment variable before running the script:

   ```bash
   export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""
   ```

   This forces TensorFlow to run on the CPU only and will help isolate whether the GPU setup is the root cause.

### 6. **Simplify the Code**
   In your code, you're using a `Sequential` model without specifying the input layer explicitly. TensorFlow should usually infer the input shape from the data, but specifying the input layer explicitly might resolve the issue. You can try this:

   ```python
   model1 = tf.keras.models.Sequential()
   model1.add(tf.keras.layers.InputLayer(input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)))
   ```

### 7. **Check Logs and Debugging**
   Given the core dump, it's useful to run your script under a debugger (like `gdb`) to get more detailed error information:

   ```bash
   gdb --args python digits_uebung.py
   ```

   After it crashes, type `bt` to get a backtrace that might reveal the specific function causing the crash.

### Conclusion
- **GPU setup**: Double-check your TensorFlow with CUDA/cuDNN installation.
- **Environment**: Consider downgrading your CUDA version or using TensorFlow nightly if you need CUDA 12.4 support.
- **Memory Management**: Enable GPU memory growth.
- **Isolation**: Test with CPU only by setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""` to narrow down the issue.

By following these steps, you should be able to resolve the issue or at least isolate the root cause. Let me know if you need more assistance!

comments.body:
The error you're encountering seems to be a combination of issues related to the CUDA environment, TensorFlow, and possibly mismatches in library versions on Manjaro. The crash (Exit Code 134, signal 6: SIGABRT) typically points to a problem in the underlying system, often a segmentation fault, memory corruption, or an internal assert failure.

Here are some steps to troubleshoot and potentially resolve the issue:

### 1. **Verify TensorFlow with GPU Setup**
   - Ensure TensorFlow can detect your GPU correctly. You can run the following snippet to check if TensorFlow sees your GPU:

   ```python
   import tensorflow as tf
   print("Num GPUs Available: ", len(tf.config.experimental.list_physical_devices('GPU')))
   ```

   If the output is `0`, it means TensorFlow is not able to access your GPU, and this could be the reason you're getting the crash.

### 2. **Check cuDNN, cuBLAS, cuFFT Initialization Issues**
   The logs suggest that TensorFlow is struggling to register cuDNN, cuBLAS, and cuFFT plugins. These are crucial for accelerated computation on NVIDIA GPUs.

   - **cuDNN Version Mismatch**: The error message about registering the cuDNN factory usually occurs when there are conflicts in the cuDNN versions installed on the system. Since you have CUDA 12.4 installed, ensure that you also have the compatible cuDNN version installed.
   
   - Try running this command to ensure you have the correct versions of both CUDA and cuDNN:
   
     ```bash
     pacman -S nvidia-cuda-toolkit nvidia-cudnn
     ```

   - **TensorFlow Compatibility**: Verify that the version of TensorFlow you're using is compatible with your installed CUDA and cuDNN versions. According to the TensorFlow release notes, TensorFlow 2.18.0 is compatible with CUDA 11.2 or 11.8. Since you're using CUDA 12.4, this could be causing issues. You might want to either:
     - Downgrade your CUDA/cuDNN version to match TensorFlow's supported versions.
     - Alternatively, try using a nightly build of TensorFlow that might support newer CUDA versions.

### 3. **Memory Issues / GPU Overload**
   The assertion error and core dump could also indicate a memory issue. The RTX 4090 is a powerful GPU, but there could still be memory overloads or memory leaks in the TensorFlow code. 

   Try limiting the GPU memory growth using the following configuration before running your TensorFlow code:

   ```python
   physical_devices = tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')
   tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth(physical_devices[0], True)
   ```

### 4. **Update TensorFlow and Dependencies**
   Ensure you're using the latest stable version of TensorFlow compatible with your system. Since you're on Manjaro, it's possible that some dependencies might be outdated or incompatible.

   Run the following commands to update your system and TensorFlow dependencies:

   ```bash
   sudo pacman -Syu        # Update system
   pip install --upgrade tensorflow
   pip install --upgrade numpy
   pip install --upgrade keras
   ```

   If you're still using the `python-tensorflow-opt-cuda` binary package from `pacman`, consider switching to the `pip`-based TensorFlow installation as the Manjaro package might be outdated or incorrectly configured.

### 5. **Testing with CPU Only**
   If the issue is specifically with GPU support, you can try disabling GPU usage temporarily to verify if the issue is related to CUDA. This can be done by setting the environment variable before running the script:

   ```bash
   export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""
   ```

   This forces TensorFlow to run on the CPU only and will help isolate whether the GPU setup is the root cause.

### 6. **Simplify the Code**
   In your code, you're using a `Sequential` model without specifying the input layer explicitly. TensorFlow should usually infer the input shape from the data, but specifying the input layer explicitly might resolve the issue. You can try this:

   ```python
   model1 = tf.keras.models.Sequential()
   model1.add(tf.keras.layers.InputLayer(input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)))
   ```

### 7. **Check Logs and Debugging**
   Given the core dump, it's useful to run your script under a debugger (like `gdb`) to get more detailed error information:

   ```bash
   gdb --args python digits_uebung.py
   ```

   After it crashes, type `bt` to get a backtrace that might reveal the specific function causing the crash.

### Conclusion
- **GPU setup**: Double-check your TensorFlow with CUDA/cuDNN installation.
- **Environment**: Consider downgrading your CUDA version or using TensorFlow nightly if you need CUDA 12.4 support.
- **Memory Management**: Enable GPU memory growth.
- **Isolation**: Test with CPU only by setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""` to narrow down the issue.

By following these steps, you should be able to resolve the issue or at least isolate the root cause. Let me know if you need more assistance!

Thank you for your confirmation. We're glad to hear that the issue has been resolved by installing TensorFlow and Keras versions `2.16.1` and `3.3.0` respectively using `pip`.

question_text: Internal error: Cannot create interpreter: Didn't find op for builtin opcode 'FULLY_CONNECTED' version '12'. An older version of this builtin might be supported. Are you using an old TFLite binary with a newer model?
answer_text:
This looks like it might be due to a mismatch between the version of TensorFlow used to build your model, and the version of TensorFlow Lite used to execute it.  In particular, are you sure that you are using version 2.17 of TF Lite?

That version of TF Lite supports versions 1 to 12 (inclusive) of the 'FULLY_CONNECTED'  op
https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/ad6d8cc177d0c868982e39e0823d0efbfb95f04c/tensorflow/lite/core/kernels/register.cc#L85
so I would not expect to see that message unless either (a) you are using an older version of TF Lite or (b) you are using an op resolver that doesn't support the 'FULLY_CONNECTED' op at all.

title: Installing tensorflow version 2.17.0 and curl is getting installed of version 7.85.0 which is outdated. Is there way to remove critical Vulnerability for curl 7.85.0.

Install tensorflow version 2.17.0 and curl is getting installed of version 7.85.0 which is outdated. Having security vulnerabilities for tensorflow-io-gcs-filesystem/tensorflow_io_gcs_filesystem-0.31.0-cp310-cp310-win_amd64.whl.

answer_text:
The mail brach has been moved from 7.85.0 to "curl-8.6.0". Could you please have a look at the below file  for the reference.
```python

    tf_http_archive(
        name = "curl",
        build_file = "//third_party:curl.BUILD",
        sha256 = "9c6db808160015f30f3c656c0dec125feb9dc00753596bf858a272b5dd8dc398",
        strip_prefix = "curl-8.6.0",
        system_build_file = "//third_party/systemlibs:curl.BUILD",
        urls = tf_mirror_urls("https://curl.se/download/curl-8.6.0.tar.gz"),
    )
```

title: TF model trained with 2.7 has error in later versions with no OpKernel error
need_summary: Whether the missing BoostedTreesBucketize kernel in newer TensorFlow versions is tied to the boosted-trees deprecation and removal noted in the v2.8.0 release note, which says to switch to TensorFlow Decision Forests or tf.searchsorted.
security_topic: applicability of deprecated boosted trees op removal across TensorFlow versions
question_text:
Hi @tilakrayal, thanks for the response! 

Based on the log, we noticed the errored model called `bucketize` transform in Tensorflow so that it touched the `BoostedTreesBucketize` op (`[[transform/transform/bucketize/apply_buckets/assign_buckets_all_shapes/assign_buckets/BoostedTreesBucketize]]`), but `bucketize` transform doesn't show as deprecated as `BoostedTreesBucketize`. Does that mean `bucketize` just started to call other substitute ops after deprecating `BoostedTreesBucketize`? 

From the [release note](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/releases/tag/v2.8.0), `BoostedTreesBucketize` appears deprecated since TF 2.8 and removed since TF 2.9: ```
Due to security issues (see section below), all boosted trees code has been deprecated. Users should switch to [TensorFlow Decision Forests](https://github.com/tensorflow/decision-forests). TF's boosted trees code will be eliminated before the branch cut for TF 2.9 and will no longer be present since that release.
```.  We tried Triton image built on TF 2.9 and this error starts to show up. Does that mean this issue can be resolved by simply switching our TF dependency for model training to TF2.9+, but still keeping the call of `bucketize`?

comments.body:
Hi @tilakrayal, thanks for the response! 

Based on the log, we noticed the errored model called `bucketize` transform in Tensorflow so that it touched the `BoostedTreesBucketize` op (`[[transform/transform/bucketize/apply_buckets/assign_buckets_all_shapes/assign_buckets/BoostedTreesBucketize]]`), but `bucketize` transform doesn't show as deprecated as `BoostedTreesBucketize`. Does that mean `bucketize` just started to call other substitute ops after deprecating `BoostedTreesBucketize`? 

From the [release note](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/releases/tag/v2.8.0), `BoostedTreesBucketize` appears deprecated since TF 2.8 and removed since TF 2.9: ```
Due to security issues (see section below), all boosted trees code has been deprecated. Users should switch to [TensorFlow Decision Forests](https://github.com/tensorflow/decision-forests). TF's boosted trees code will be eliminated before the branch cut for TF 2.9 and will no longer be present since that release.
```.  We tried Triton image built on TF 2.9 and this error starts to show up. Does that mean this issue can be resolved by simply switching our TF dependency for model training to TF2.9+, but still keeping the call of `bucketize`?
